_comment: What each operation costs, in credits. One credit is one penny.
An operation is charged when it costs this instance something to run: a
model call to somebody we pay, or a third party billed per request.
Anything that only touches this instance's own storage is 0, because it
has no marginal cost and charging for it taxed exactly the behaviour the
product wants more of. Abuse control for those is auth.CheckPostRate,
not the price.
Talking to your agent is 0 as well, and that is a product decision rather
than an arithmetic one. The agent is the thing you came for; metering it
meant a new account could not ask a question until it had paid, which is
why there used to be a daily grant of credits here to cancel the charge
back out. Both are gone. What bounds it now is `limit` — a count of runs
a day, which is abuse control and not a price.
A price is what a *fetch* costs. A call the instance answered from
something it already had — a cached forecast, a stored tile — is not
charged; see internal/service/meter.go. So the busier a shared instance
is, the less its callers pay.
`limit` is a hard count per account per day, separate from money and
checked before it. It is the second control for the three operations that
reach a stranger — a price stops somebody who has to pay and does nothing
about a loop, and what a loop spends there is a domain's or a number's
reputation, which no balance repairs.
This is an operator's file. Edit it, or drop a quota.json in the data
directory to override without rebuilding.

operations.label: Travel time between two places
operations.note: routes_eta. Google Routes, 0.38p at Essentials (£3.76/1k after 10k free), 0.75p at Pro. We ask for traffic, which may bill at Pro — priced to cover it. The op id keeps the old name so an operator's existing override and usage history survive the rename

operations.label: Turn-by-turn directions
operations.note: Google Routes asking for steps and the road's shape, which is more than an ETA and bills higher — 1.14p at Enterprise

operations.label: Summarise text
operations.note: Atlas deepseek-v4-flash ($0.14/$0.28 per M). 0.10p at the 30k cap — a 21x markup, 160x on a typical call

operations.label: Extract structure from text
operations.note: Atlas deepseek-v4-pro ($1.68/$3.38 per M) because a wrong field is silent. 1.28p at the 30k cap — was 3, which left only 2.4x

operations.label: Classify text
operations.note: Atlas deepseek-v4-flash, output is one word. 0.09p at the 30k cap — the cheapest real model call here

operations.label: Translate text
operations.note: Atlas deepseek-v4-flash. Output is as long as the input, so on pro this cost 3.46p at the cap against a 3p price — the one loss-making path. On flash, 0.29p and a 10x markup

operations.label: App build (AI)
operations.note: Was 100 — a pound, six times the next most expensive thing on the menu, for less model than an agent run

operations.label: App edit (AI)
operations.note: The model call only. Manual editing at /apps/<slug>/edit is free

operations.label: WhatsApp conversation
operations.note: Twilio bills WhatsApp by the 24-hour conversation rather than the message, so this is charged once per window and the rest of the thread is free. Cheaper than a text because it costs us less and cannot be sent cold — the other person has to write first

operations.label: Text message (per segment)
operations.note: Twilio: under a penny to a US mobile, ~4p to a UK one, and charged per 160-character segment. A markup that would be silly on a search is the point here — a text cannot be unsent, and the number's reputation is shared by everybody on the instance. Ten pence makes a spam run cost real money before any of the other limits are reached

operations.label: Send message
operations.note: Local user to local user. "Message" not "mail": sending a real email is charged as external_email
